title: Effectiveness of a Generate–Verify–Repair Pipeline with Batfish for LLM‑Generated Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We report a preregistered, paired confirmatory experiment (study id cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1) that measured whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—shared initial LLM candidate (gpt-5-mini) + deterministic Batfish‑style validator + at most one automated LLM repair—reduces verifier‑detected semantic/safety failures for intent→vendor‑CLI NetOps tasks. The preregistered design planned N=300 intent pairs; after infrastructure exclusions 266 paired units completed. Baseline initial candidate passes: 260/266 (97.744%). Final guarded (GVR) passes: 265/266 (99.624%). Paired difference = 0.01879699 (1.88 percentage points); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625; paired bootstrap (B=10,000, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.0037594, 0.03759398]. Repair invocation was rare (6 recorded repair calls). Under the preregistered primary decision rule (exact McNemar at α=0.05) the observed improvement does not reach confirmatory significance; the bootstrap CI is positive but interpretive caution is required because discordant counts are very small. We present the preregistered design, deterministic validation rules, recorded runtime model settings, primary confirmatory result, and a focused discussion of operational implications and validity threats; all execution and analysis artifacts are archived (execution manifest and analysis artifacts referenced in the paper).

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation and zero‑touch configuration generation [1,2]. Stochastic LLM output can produce syntactic or semantic violations (hallucinations) that risk unsafe network states; this motivates grounded pipelines that interpose deterministic validators and bounded repair loops [3]. We ask: does a preregistered GVR pipeline that uses an LLM for initial generation, a deterministic network validator (Batfish‑style), and at most one automated repair invocation reduce verifier‑detected failures relative to the shared initial candidate? Our contribution is (1) a preregistered paired experiment (study id cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1) executed end‑to‑end with archived artifacts, (2) a transparent confirmatory analysis of the primary paired estimand, and (3) an evidence‑grounded interpretation of practical and validity implications. Key practical constraint: under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics both baseline and guarded conditions began from the same model output; any paired difference therefore arises only from the validator‑triggered guarded repair.
sections.related_work: Prior work documents prototype and benchmark efforts that translate intent into vendor CLI or API artifacts and proposes validator‑centric or GVR architectures for improving correctness [2,1,3]. Survey and analytic studies emphasize LLM grounding techniques (RAG, tool augmentation, constrained decoding) and document hallucination risks in domain‑constrained tasks, motivating verifier integration [2,4]. Network verification tools (Batfish and related header‑space analyses) are standard validator candidates and have been advocated as LLM‑pipeline oracles [5]. Our work differs by executing a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired test that directly measures the guarded (validator+repair) effect under shared_initial_candidate semantics on a deterministically generated task corpus.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study plan (cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1) fixed the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, a shared_initial_candidate paired design, and a planned N=300 intent pairs (150 Cisco‑like, 150 Juniper‑like from public examples and a deterministic synthetic generator). Execution contract: exactly one initial LLM generation per task; if deterministic validation failed, the guarded pipeline could invoke at most one automated repair call. Deterministic validation: the evaluator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (Batfish‑style checks) performs syntactic parsing, required‑sequence and reachability checks, and emits pass/fail with violation codes; tests used its categorical pass/fail output as the binary outcome. Recorded runtime model settings (from execution/model_configuration.json): declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini; max_output_tokens = 1024; maximum_attempts_per_call = 1; provider = openai_responses; temperature = null (unset in the recorded configuration). A null/empty temperature setting in the manifest does not itself imply deterministic sampling and no explicit deterministic seed was recorded; therefore sampling nondeterminism cannot be excluded and is disclosed. Inclusion/exclusion and missingness: preregistered retry rules allowed up to two automatic retries for transient provider failures; irrecoverable model/API failures produced logged episode exclusions per the preregistered missingness plan. Execution accounting: planned episodes 600; completed episodes 532; complete paired units after exclusions 266. Reproducibility: all raw model outputs, validator traces, provider call logs, task manifests, and analysis artifacts are archived and referenced in the execution manifest.
sections.results: Primary confirmatory outcome (predefined exact test): among 266 complete pairs baseline initial candidates passed deterministic validation in 260 cases (97.744%) and the final guarded outcome passed in 265 cases (99.624%). Paired contingency (guarded,baseline): n11=260, n10=5, n01=0, n00=1. Paired difference estimate = 0.018796992481203034. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625 (preregistered primary decision rule α=0.05). Paired bootstrap percentile CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) = [0.0037594, 0.03759398] (reported for descriptive context; the preregistered confirmatory decision follows the McNemar result). Repair activity: provider_call_audit(stage_counts) records shared_initial_generation = 300 and repair = 6, i.e., six repair calls were executed in the run. Missingness: 34 episodes failed due to provider/infrastructure errors and were excluded per the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' plan; missingness_summary.csv is archived. The preregistered sensitivity analysis that would treat failed episodes as failures was not executed in the primary analysis pipeline and hence is not reported as a confirmatory numeric result (see Limitations). Additional archived artifacts include condition_summary.csv, paired_contingency_table.csv, and the deterministic execution manifest.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: the guarded pipeline produced a small absolute increase in verifier pass rate (~1.9 percentage points). Under the preregistered exact McNemar test this difference does not reach α=0.05 (p=0.0625). The bootstrap CI reported above lies entirely positive; the divergence between the exact McNemar p‑value and the bootstrap CI stems from the very small number of discordant pairs (n10=5, n01=0). Exact McNemar inference on sparse discordants is discrete and can yield a non‑significant two‑sided p even when a resampling CI excludes zero; this is an inferential nuance rather than a data mismatch. Operationally, the low repair invocation rate (6 repairs) indicates that for this task set and model the initial candidates were already highly likely to satisfy the deterministic validator, limiting headroom for the guarded pipeline to improve outcomes. Implications and caveats: GVR with a deterministic validator can provide deterministic assurance and a bounded repair mechanism, but marginal benefit will depend on baseline failure rate, validator coverage, vendor dialect complexity, and the frequency of repairable semantic errors. Our shared_initial_candidate design means we measured only validator‑triggered repair benefit, not the effect of alternate constrained‑prompting strategies that would produce independent initial candidates.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment testing whether a GVR pipeline (gpt-5-mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5 + a single automated repair attempt) reduces verifier‑detected failures for intent→CLI NetOps tasks. Across 266 completed pairs the guarded pipeline yielded an absolute increase of 0.01880 (1.88 percentage points) in final verifier pass rate; under the preregistered exact McNemar test this did not meet α=0.05 (p=0.0625). Repair invocations were rare (6), indicating limited opportunity for repair on this corpus and model. We archive all artifacts and emphasize the need for broader evaluations across vendor dialects, larger topologies, and higher baseline failure regimes to fully characterize practical benefits of GVR pipelines. Interpretive caution is warranted given the small discordant counts and the omitted preregistered sensitivity step (see Limitations).

limitations: Sample and missingness: planned N=300 pairs; after infrastructure/API exclusions 266 pairs completed and 34 episodes were lost and excluded per the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' rule—this reduces effective sample size and precision.

Sensitivity analysis omitted: the preregistered sensitivity analysis that would treat failed episodes/pairs as failures was not executed in the primary analysis pipeline and therefore no alternative paired numeric result is reported here; omission is disclosed as a limitation and a candidate for follow‑up analysis using the archived artifacts.

Design scope and external validity: tasks were intent→CLI scenarios drawn from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a deterministic synthetic generator limited to two vendor‑dialect clusters; results do not imply universal GVR benefit across other vendors, larger topologies, or production environments.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: both baseline and guarded conditions began from the same initial generation; measured effect is strictly the validator‑triggered repair benefit and does not evaluate independent constrained‑prompt generations or alternative first‑pass strategies.

Validator coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 provides a finite set of syntactic/semantic/reachability checks; undetected semantic violations outside the validator's coverage are possible and not measured.

Small discordant counts: primary inference relied on exact McNemar with very few discordant pairs (n10=5, n01=0); interpretive conclusions are sensitive to inferential choice (see Results and Discussion).

Runtime sampling settings: recorded execution/model_configuration.json shows temperature = null (unset) and no explicit deterministic seed; null does not imply deterministic sampling and nondeterminism cannot be excluded from the execution manifest.
